1. Determining the sample’s composition: analytical chemistry.
2. Studying the physical properties of its materials: physical chemistry.
3. Reactions with usual inorganic reagents: inorganic chemistry.

Chemistry is a broad and complex subject, so it is divided into branches to make it easier to study. The branches let scientists focus on particular areas and develop expertise. This specialization also supports further research and advances in chemistry.
Reactions involving electrons outside the nucleus are studied in the other branches of chemistry, while reactions inside the nucleus are studied in nuclear chemistry.
Analytical chemistry deals with separating, identifying and determining the amounts or concentrations of the components in a sample.

Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, including their structures, properties and reactions. Biochemistry focuses on the chemical substances and processes in living organisms, even though many of these substances are organic.

(a) Physical chemistry
(b) Biochemistry
(c) Physical chemistry
(d) Environmental chemistry
(e) Inorganic chemistry
(f) Analytical chemistry

Inorganic chemistry mainly studies elements and compounds that contain little or no carbon. Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, excluding simple compounds such as carbonates, bicarbonates, oxides and carbides.
